Webinar ISCN · 14 August 2026 · Online

SDGs Alignment of Indonesia’s Research Strength

Arief Anshory Yusuf

Bio

Arief Anshory Yusuf is Professor of Economics at Padjadjaran University, Indonesia, where he works on development economics. He is also Visiting Professor at King’s College London, Honorary Senior Lecturer at the Australian National University, and Non-resident Senior Research Fellow at UNU-WIDER. He holds a Bachelor in Economics from Padjadjaran University, an MSc from University College London, and a PhD from the Australian National University. He is a member of Indonesia’s National Economic Council (2024–2029), advising the President on strategic economic issues.

Indonesia’s universities publish a great deal on the SDGs. The question is whether they publish on the goals their own provinces are failing.

Method

How the dashboard measures research strength

SDG Center UNPAD's public dashboard maps Indonesia's highest-quality research output onto the 17 goals. Live at sdgcenter.unpad.ac.id/dashboard since 18 June 2026.

1

Corpus

75,892 Q1 journal articles with an Indonesian affiliation, 2015 onwards, downloaded from the Scopus API. Articles only; discontinued titles excluded.

2

Mapping to goals

Matched to goals by the Elsevier Aurora keyword framework. 32,257 papers carry a tag; one paper can match several goals, so shares exceed 100%.

3

Classing the goals

Each goal's share is classed Strong (≥5%), Moderate (1–5%) or Gap (<1%) — the dashboard's own threshold.

4

Institutions

Co-authorship frequency: a paper counts once per institution. Universities only; agencies and hospitals excluded.

5

Concentration

Gini and Lorenz across all 2,571 universities, from the paper records — the published top-25 lists are too short to describe a distribution.

What the method cannot do

Keyword tagging mis-assigns. 25.7% of output tagged SDG 9 was education research caught by the word innovation.

The Q1 filter is not neutral. Equity and urban research skews to national journals it excludes by construction.

Quartiles are field-normalised. Q1 in a small category is a lower bar.

Source & method
Scopus Search API (Elsevier), June 2026; SCImago Journal Rank 2025; Elsevier discontinued-title list, May 2026; Elsevier/Aurora SDG keyword framework. Goal shares and institutional counts are taken from the figures the dashboard itself publishes. Its CSV export disagrees with those figures on the leading institution in 6 of the 17 goals — the export does not merge Universitas Indonesia's name variants and teaching hospital into the parent. The published figures are used throughout.

Figure 4

Five goals carry the output; four are near-absent

Share of Indonesia's 75,892 Q1 papers addressing each SDG, with paper counts. Four goals fall below the 1% line the dashboard uses to flag a research gap.

Source & method
Partnerships for the Goals is the smallest at 286 papers over eleven years. Because a paper may carry several SDG tags, the shares sum to more than 100% and are not slices of a pie.

Figure 5

Which university leads a goal tracks what that university is for

Rank of each producer within each SDG. ITB's block sits on water, energy and consumption; IPB's on climate, marine and land; UI and Unair hold health. The two teacher-training universities are absent from every goal but one — Quality Education, which they lead.

ranked 1st in the goal2nd–3rd4th–5th6th–10thoutside the top 10
Source & method
Ranks are by co-authorship count, so Universitas Indonesia leads on volume in eight of the seventeen goals. What tracks institutional mandate is the specialists: ITB and IPB hold coherent blocks, and the teacher-training universities appear in one goal only.

Figure 6

Productivity and breadth pick out different leaders

Publication volume against the number of the 17 goals in which a university ranks in the top ten. UI and UGM lead on both; Unpad is broad without the volume; ITB and IPB are productive but narrow.

Source & method
Breadth is top-ten membership, so it partly measures size — a university has to be large enough to enter a top-ten list at all. It is informative as a contrast between institutions of similar size, less so as an absolute.

Figure 7

Expertise is extraordinarily concentrated

Cumulative share of Q1 SDG output across the 2,571 universities that appear at all, poorest to richest. The diagonal is perfect equality.

0.89Gini coefficient across 2,571 universities
38%of all Q1 SDG output held by the top ten institutions
1,450universities — 56% of those appearing at all — appear on exactly one paper in eleven years
Source & method
Computed from the dashboard's own downloaded paper records, applying its own universities-only filter. The Gini of 0.89 independently reproduces the figure obtained from an OpenAlex corpus over the same period.

Method

How research quality was measured

978,546 journal articles and reviews indexed to Indonesian institutions on OpenAlex, 2015–2026, with no topic filter, cross-classified against Scopus.

1

Journal quality

Every source matched by ISSN against the Scopus CiteScore quartile list, May 2026 — Q1 to Q4, delisted, indexed-but-unranked, or not indexed at all.

2

Coverage check

OpenAlex's register tested against Elsevier's own API: 250 randomly drawn “not in Scopus” journals came back zero false negatives. A reliable census of the literature.

3

Institution check

Not a reliable authority on who wrote it. Three of the 25 largest records — sharing templates like IAIN X — conflate a whole class of institutions. Established universities matched at 92–99%, these three at 1–6%. All excluded.

4

Ranking

The 25 largest remaining producers, ranked twice over the same period: once by total output, once by Q1-only output.

Source & method
OpenAlex works metadata (2015–2026), Scopus CiteScore quartile list (May 2026), and the Scopus Sources API, used to verify OpenAlex's journal register directly.

Figure 3

Counting everything inverts the ranking

Only 5.2% of the 978,546 works reach a Q1 journal. Institutions that gain ground under the quality filter are named; those that lose ground are shown as letters, held consistent across both columns.

Source & method
Indonesia's 25 largest research producers by OpenAlex works count, 2015–2026, with the three misattributed institution records excluded (see Method). UI, UGM and Universitas Airlangga hold the top three places on both sides — the very top of Indonesian research is stable. Institut Teknologi Bandung climbs 18→4; Universitas Negeri Padang falls 6→17.

Method

How alignment was measured

Supply and demand are ranked over the same 16 goals for each of the 34 provinces, then compared.

1

Supply

Scopus publication counts per SDG for 457 Indonesian universities, attributed to the province the university sits in. Each province's five strongest goals are its supply.

2

Measured demand

285 official indicator-dimensions from the National SDGs Secretariat, aggregated by principal component analysis into a 0–100 achievement index. Each province's five weakest goals are its demand.

3

Stated demand

A survey of provincial Bappeda, February–March 2025, answered by 27 of 34 provinces — their own declared priorities. With focus groups and content analysis of all 34 provincial RPJMDs.

4

Alignment

A goal on both lists is a match — a development gap the province's own universities are already strong in.

Source & method
SDG Center Business Model final report (2025), §2, Table 4-22 and Figure 4-1. Figure 1 carries both demand measures; Figure 2 carries only the revealed one, because the survey has no per-province breakdown. Supply is measured by university location, not by where the research is about.

Figure 1

Where universities are strong, where provinces are failing, and what provinces say they want

All 16 goals, ordered by the gap between revealed demand and supply. Demand is measured twice, from two different sources.

Supply — a top-5 university strengthRevealed demand — a bottom-5 achievementStated demand — survey priority rank
Source & method
Panel 1 from Table 4-22, counted across all 34 provinces. Panel 2 from the Bappeda survey (Figure 4-1), a mean rank across the 27 provinces that responded — it has no per-province breakdown, which is why it appears as its own panel rather than sharing panel 1's axis. Life below water is a bottom-five achievement in 30 of 34 provinces and a stated priority of 14.2 out of 16; no poverty is the mirror image.

Figure 2

Province by province, goal by goal

Each row is a province, each column an SDG. Green is a match: a goal that is both one of the province's five strongest by publication and one of its five weakest by achievement.

Both — strength meets needSupply onlyNeed onlyNeither
Source & method
Built from Table 4-22, provinces in the report's order. Column 9 is almost solid orange — industry and infrastructure is a gap nearly everywhere and a strength almost nowhere; columns 3 and 7 run the other way.

Implications

What follows for policy

Six recommendations, each resting on a specific figure in this deck rather than on general good practice.

1

Stop ranking on volume

Counting everything inverts the ranking — ITB moves 18→4 once quality is applied. Rules keyed to raw counts reward the wrong institutions and feed the 78.8% of output no index carries. Report volume and quality separately, never merged.

Figure 3
2

Commission the blind spots

Gender, inequality, cities and partnerships each sit below 1%, and no institution has claimed any as a niche. That is a gap in incentives, not capability — it needs earmarked calls, not general capacity funds.

Figure 4
3

Match goals to mandates

Strength follows institutional purpose: ITB on energy, water and cities; IPB on land, climate and marine; the LPTK on education. Use the mapping platform to match provincial need to the institution whose mandate fits, rather than asking all 17 goals of everyone.

Figure 5 · report rec. 4
4

Academic mobility and professor exchange

Ten institutions hold 38% of frontier output while 1,450 universities appear on a single paper. A national visiting-professor and sabbatical scheme moves capability to where it is thin faster than building it from nothing.

Figure 7
5

A national consortium of SDG Centers

SDG 17 is the weakest goal at 0.38% and simultaneously the instrument for the rest. Inter-provincial collaboration, joint research agendas and consortium authorship are how the tail reaches the frontier.

Figure 4 · report rec. 3
6

Institutionalise and finance the relationship

Put SDG Centers into local planning and budgeting through MoUs or service contracts, backed by a national financing framework — budget allocation, donor guidelines, and incentives for universities to sustain SDG units.

Report rec. 1 & 5
Source & method
Recommendations 1, 2 and 4 follow from the figures in this deck. Recommendations 3, 5 and 6 restate or extend the strategic recommendations of the SDG Center Business Model — Final Report (2025), §5, prepared for the Asian Development Bank. Two further recommendations of that report — a hybrid academic/think-tank business model, and minimum service standards with professional certification for Center staff — concern the running of the Centers rather than the research itself and are not shown here.
Sources. SDGs Research Dashboard, SDG Center UNPAD (Scopus, June 2026), for the coverage, leadership and concentration figures. OpenAlex and Scopus, 2015–2026, for the quality-filter figure.
